newsitem.title: ISRAEL: YEAREND - Middle East peace process limps into 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Middle East peace process limps into 1997.

text.p: After a year of ballots, bombs and bullets, the Middle East peace process is still on its feet but only able to limp into 1997.
Just over a year ago Israelis and Palestinians were marching towards a settlement of their conflict and the Jewish state stood ready for a Golan compromise with arch-enemy Syria.

But the assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, Palestinian suicide bombers, Israel's lurch to the right in elections and gunbattles between Israeli and PLO security forces have hobbled the peace process.

Diplomats believe U.S, President Bill Clinton's second term administration might invite Middle East leaders to Washington next spring in an effort to quicken the pace of PLO-Israeli talks and restart Israeli contacts with Damascus.
BETTER CHANCES WITH PLO THAN SYRIA
The chances of success are greater on the Israeli-PLO track than the Syrian, diplomats say. But even there success will be defined as keeping the sides talking rather than making progress.

All sides agree that Israel and the Palestinian Authority will eventually overcome differences delaying an Israel troop redeployment in Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns to be handed over to Palestinian rule under the 1993 Olso accord.
Right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has little choice but to honour the internationally-sponsored self-rule agreements signed by Rabin, including a pullback from 80 percent of Hebron.
The problem from the Palestinian perspective is how far and how fast Netanyahu will withdraw from the remainder of the West Bank and Gaza still under occupation.
"Netanyahu will grant them as much control over daily life as he can," says Zeev Maoz, head of the Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies. "But he will be tough on two issues, security and statehood."

Netanyahu, who has to hold together a coalition that includes right-wing idealogues and Jewish settlers, will insist on tighter overall control of security and maintain his opposition to PLO leader Yasser Arafat's goal of a Palestinian state, Maoz said.

"I think it's a strategy that will backfire," Maoz said. A breakthrough on Hebron would provide relief but eventually Netanyahu would have to reveal his position on the thorny "final status" issues left for the last phase of Oslo, such as the status of Jerusalem and return of Palestinian refugees.
"Here the Palestinians will realise there is no movement," Maoz said.
Ghassan Khatib, a Palestinian analyst and critic of Oslo, agrees.

"Netanyahu must show the United States and outside world that he is committed to Oslo," Khatib said, arguing that the Likud party leader does not want to risk Israel's budding economic prosperity and ties with Arab and Moslem states, both of which have soured since his election.
But Khatib expects little Israeli movement on final status issues before Netanyahu seeks re-election in four years' time.
"Israel wants peace with the Arabs without paying the price -- a Palestinian state," Khatib said.
NETANYAHU COMING TO TERMS WITH EX-ENEMIES

Sources close to Netanyahu say that, after a shaky start this summer with Arafat, the prime minister and his team of untested advisers are overcoming their aversion to dealing with their former enemies.
"Both Israel and the PLO have invested too much in Oslo to backtrack now," said one source. "In '97 we'll muddle through."

The pace of implementation may not be enough to avoid the violence born of frustrated aspirations and economic hardship that have marked some of the outbursts in 1996. Other attacks, such as bus bombings last February and March, stand for outright political and religious opposition to Israel.
"If Oslo is not implemented, I'm afraid we'll see explosions," said Mahmoud Abbas, Arafat's right-hand man.
Maoz thinks that, even after a Hebron deal, violence between the city's tiny militant Jewish settler population and Arabs is possible.
"Hebron is a powderkeg with a very short fuse," Maoz said.
A Hebron agreement will help Israel's strained relations with Egypt, Jordan and other Arab states, political analysts say, but few expect a resumption of real negotiations with Syria and Lebanon.
"The United States will be working to bring the parties together, if only for a get-to-know meeting," a Western envoy said.
Substantive talks seem unlikely, however, unless Netanyahu endorses the previous Labour government's land-for-peace formula.
